extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and commercial-fiction novelists (writers of thrillers and other plot-driven genres)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for plotting and structuring commercial/genre novels using James Scott Bell's LOCK system and a three-act framework, plus scene/sequel pacing and practical writer habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead (LOCK System)
rubrics_metrics.description: A protagonist worth following — sympathetic, vulnerable, with a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lead must be someone readers care about; vulnerability and a clear personal problem create sympathy and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective (LOCK System)
rubrics_metrics.description: What the lead wants — a clear, urgent goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protagonist's objective should be specific and urgent enough to drive plot forward; clarity of want creates momentum and reader investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confrontation (LOCK System)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forces of opposition sufficient to test the lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opposition must be strong, escalating, and capable of realistically challenging the protagonist, producing stakes and conflict throughout the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knockout (LOCK System)
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfying, decisive ending that resolves the central conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial fiction requires a real, satisfying resolution — no anti-climax. The knockout should decisively answer the story's central question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-Act Structure (Bell's version)
rubrics_metrics.description: Act 1 (≈1/4): establish lead and world, inciting incident, pass through first doorway of no return; Act 2 (≈1/2): confrontation, rising obstacles, midpoint reversal, second doorway; Act 3 (≈1/4): climax and resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the approximate proportions (25% / 50% / 25%) as beats for plotting; include inciting incident and midpoint reversal to reorient stakes and momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doorway 1 (first doorway of no return)
rubrics_metrics.description: Around 20–25% into the story the lead crosses into the main story and cannot go back.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the point of no return that commits the protagonist to the primary conflict — mark it clearly so the story's forward motion is inevitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doorway 2 (second doorway of no return)
rubrics_metrics.description: Around 75–80% in the lead commits to the final action; from here there is only forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doorway signals the protagonist's full commitment to the climax; it sets the stage for the final confrontation and knockout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open with action or conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin the story with action or conflict; avoid opening on weather or backstory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with the lead already in trouble or facing an inciting moment to hook readers instantly; defer backstory and exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the lead sympathetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure readers care about the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sympathy comes from vulnerability, relatable desires, and stakes that affect the lead personally; without it, reader engagement drops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the stakes personal
rubrics_metrics.description: Personalize the stakes so 'save-the-world' plots still feel emotionally grounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie external stakes to the protagonist's emotional life or relationships; large-scale stakes need a personal tether to feel meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build conflict constantly
rubrics_metrics.description: Every scene needs tension; even quiet scenes should have undercurrents of conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid neutral or purely expository scenes. Ensure each scene either advances the external plot or deepens internal conflict/tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve, don't trail off (Knockout emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliver a real, satisfying ending rather than an ambiguous or trailing conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial fiction rewards a decisive resolution to the central conflict; readers expect closure rather than ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing via Scene/Sequel alternation
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternate 'scene' (action) and 'sequel' (reaction) units to vary pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenes for goal/conflict/setback and sequels for reaction/dilemma/decision; this alternation maintains momentum while allowing character reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene structure: goal/conflict/setback
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene should present a goal, meet conflict, and end with a setback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design each active scene around a clear immediate goal and meaningful obstacle so the story keeps advancing through complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequel structure: reaction/dilemma/decision
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequel provides reaction to the scene, internal dilemma, and leads to a decision that sets the next goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequels allow characters to process events and choose next actions; ensure decisions escalate stakes and propel to the next scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality test — sympathetic lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the lead sympathetic?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a checklist prompt during revision; confirms the protagonist elicits reader care (overlaps with 'Make the lead sympathetic').

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality test — clear and urgent objective
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the protagonist's objective clear and urgent?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A quick revision check: if the objective is fuzzy or low-stakes, refocus scenes to sharpen urgency (overlaps with 'Objective').

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality test — strong opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the forces of opposition strong enough?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure antagonists/obstacles challenge the lead meaningfully; weak opposition undermines tension (overlaps with 'Confrontation').

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality test — knockout effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the knockout deliver a satisfying resolution?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the ending for decisiveness and emotional payoff; rework any anti-climactic or unresolved endings (overlaps with 'Knockout').

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality test — scene & sequel structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Are scenes structured (goal/conflict/setback) and sequels structured (reaction/dilemma/decision)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a structural checklist when editing to ensure pacing and momentum (overlaps with scene/sequel entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality test — doorways crossed
rubrics_metrics.description: Have both doorways of no return been crossed at the appropriate story points?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm the story has a clear first doorway (~20–25%) and second doorway (~75–80%) to maintain forward momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability: commercial-fiction emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Bell's advice is geared toward commercial/plot-driven fiction (especially thrillers); less applicable to literary fiction which may prize ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply LOCK and rigid doorways more flexibly if writing literary or experimental fiction; for genre work, follow them closely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing habit — daily output target
rubrics_metrics.description: Write ~350 words/day to produce a novel in a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical productivity goal for sustained progress; adjust target to individual workflow but maintain consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing habit — 'write hot' then 'edit cold'
rubrics_metrics.description: First draft should be written energetically ('hot'), then edited later ('cold').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate drafting and revision phases to preserve momentum and allow more objective editing later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading practice — read in and outside your genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Read widely: in your genre and outside it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading both within and beyond your genre informs craft, offers models, and helps innovate while meeting reader expectations.
